Practice

Learn to recognize the problem. Build a plan. Solve with confidence.

The biggest challenge in microeconomics isn’t always the math. It’s knowing where to start.

There are four main types of problems covered in this guide, and each follows a predictable process. Once you recognize which type you’re working with, you can follow the same steps every time.

Our first rule: before solving anything, write down what you know. Organizing your information is the first step toward solving the problem.

1

Recognize your problem type

Look for…What you’re solvingYour strategy
One consumer who also owns the firm Pareto optimality and competitive equilibrium System 1consumer + firm
Two goods produced using one input Returns to scale and the PPF System 2one-input PPF
Two goods, two inputs, both using Leontief production Efficient allocations and a kinked PPF System 3Leontief + Leontief
Two goods, two inputs, one Leontief and one linear production function Efficient allocations and a straight-line PPF System 4Leontief + linear

Study tip: Before you work through the algebra, identify the system. Learning to recognize the structure of a problem will save you time and help prevent mistakes.

2

System 1: One consumer + one firm

Goal: Find the Pareto-optimal allocation and the competitive equilibrium.

1

Consumer + firm

Pareto optimal? Competitive equilibrium?
  • 1Organize your givens. Write down the utility function $U(n, x)$, the production function $x = f(n)$, and the budget constraint $x = wn + \pi$. Then calculate the marginal rate of substitution ($MRS$) and the marginal product of labor ($MPL$).
  • 2Identify what you’re solving. (A) Pareto optimality or (B) competitive equilibrium?
A · Pareto optimality

Think: what allocation maximizes utility given what the economy can produce?

1. Start with $MRS = MPL$.
2. Substitute the production function to eliminate consumption.
3. Solve for optimal labor.
4. Plug back in to find consumption.

B · Competitive equilibrium

Think: what happens when the consumer and the firm make their decisions separately?

1. Consumer: $MRS = w$.
2. Firm: $MPL = w$.
3. Combine the equations: $MRS = MPL$.
4. Solve for labor, consumption, and the wage.
5. Calculate profit last.

What to remember. Both methods produce the same allocation under the assumptions of this model, but they take different routes.

For competitive equilibrium, you don’t need to repeat all your algebra from the Pareto problem. Show why the two conditions are equivalent, then use your earlier result.

Always check: does your consumption equal your labor income plus your profit? $\;x = wn + \pi$

3

System 2: Building a PPF from one input

Goal: Determine what combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its available resources.

2

One-input PPF

$x = f(L_x)$, $y = g(L_y)$, total $L$
  • 1Start with the resource constraint. $$L_x + L_y = L$$ This tells us how much labor we have available.
  • 2Rearrange each production function. Solve each production function for the amount of labor required to produce that good. The goal is to rewrite both labor inputs in terms of outputs.
  • 3Substitute into your resource constraint. Replace $L_x$ and $L_y$ with the expressions you found. You should now have an equation relating the two outputs. That’s your PPF.
  • 4Find the intercepts. Give all available labor to good $x$: how much can you produce? Give all available labor to good $y$: how much can you produce? These are the endpoints of your PPF.
  • 5Sketch and check. Use your intercepts and the equation to sketch the PPF. Check whether the shape makes sense.
Returns to scale reminder

For a Cobb-Douglas production function, add the input exponents:

Sum less than 1: decreasing returns to scale
Sum equal to 1: constant returns to scale
Sum greater than 1: increasing returns to scale

Study tip

Don’t try to memorize what the PPF looks like. Practice deriving it from the resource constraint. That strategy works even when the production functions change.

4

System 3: Leontief + Leontief

Goal: Find technologically efficient input allocations and construct the kinked PPF.

3

Box: $\min$ + $\min$

two inputs, both firms Leontief
  • 1Draw your Edgeworth box. Label total labor and capital. Firm $x$ measures inputs from the bottom-left corner; firm $y$ measures inputs from the top-right corner. The resources allocated to the two firms must add up to the economy’s totals: $L_y = L - L_x$, $K_y = K - K_x$.
  • 2Find each firm’s kink line. For each Leontief production function, set the two expressions inside the minimum function equal. This tells you the input combinations where that firm uses labor and capital in exactly the required proportions.
  • 3Put both conditions in the same variables. Use the resource constraints to rewrite firm $y$’s kink line in terms of firm $x$’s inputs. Now you can compare both lines in the same diagram.
  • 4Identify efficient allocations. Find where the kink lines intersect. Then identify the full efficient region between the two kink lines. The intersection is an important point, but it is not the only efficient allocation.
  • 5Construct the PPF. Determine how much labor and capital are needed to produce each unit of output. Build two constraints: one based on total labor, one based on total capital. The feasible output combinations must satisfy both. The PPF follows the more restrictive constraint at each level of output.
  • 6Find intercepts and the kink. Maximize production of each good separately to find the endpoints. Then solve where the two resource constraints intersect to locate the kink.

Study tip: Work on one constraint at a time. Draw the box, find the kink lines, and only then move to the PPF.

5

System 4: Leontief + linear

Goal: Find efficient input allocations and construct the PPF when one firm uses fixed input proportions and the other can substitute between inputs.

4

Box: $\min$ + straight line

one firm Leontief, one firm $aL + bK$
  • 1Draw the box. Start exactly as you did in System 3. Label your total resources and both firms’ origins.
  • 2Find the Leontief firm’s kink line. Set the two expressions inside the minimum equal. The linear firm doesn’t have a kink line.
  • 3Identify efficient allocations. For the positive input coefficients in these linear production technologies, efficient allocations follow the Leontief firm’s kink line up to the feasible endpoint. Check whether the kink line reaches the box’s far corner or stops at a resource boundary.
  • 4Build the PPF. 1. Express the Leontief firm’s input requirements in terms of its output. 2. Subtract those requirements from the economy’s total resources. 3. Allocate the remaining inputs to the linear firm. 4. Substitute into the linear production function. 5. Simplify to get the PPF.
  • 5Check the endpoints. Find the maximum output of each good by allocating all resources to one firm at a time. For these production functions, your PPF should be a straight line.
6

Algebra guardrails

No fractions

When an equation has fractions on both sides, multiply everything by the product of the denominators before solving. $\;\tfrac{2}{3}n^{-1/3} = \tfrac12\;$ → times 6 → $\;4n^{-1/3} = 3$. Now there is nothing to divide wrong.

Roots

$n^{1/3} = \tfrac43$ means $n = \left(\tfrac43\right)^3 = \tfrac{64}{27}$, not $\tfrac43$. $n^{-1/3} = \tfrac34$ means $n^{1/3} = \tfrac43$ first (flip), then cube. $\sqrt n = 2$ means $n = 4$.

One variable at a time

Whenever an equation has both $x$ and $n$, plug $x = f(n)$ in so only $n$ is left. For the box, plug the cross-over in so only $L_x, K_x$ are left. Never carry two unknowns if you can carry one.

Check by maxing out

Every PPF ends on the axes. Giving everything to one good must land exactly on your curve’s intercept. If it doesn’t, the algebra slipped somewhere in steps 2–4.

1

Worked example: the four-step process

worked example

Worked example 1. One individual is both the consumer/worker and the owner of the firm. $U(n,x) = x - \tfrac{n}{2}$ (linear). The firm produces $x = n^{1/2}$.

(a) Pareto optimal $n$ and $x$.   (b) With $x$ as numeraire and wage $w$: competitive equilibrium $x$, $n$, $w$, and profit.   (c) New technology $x = n^{2/3}$: Pareto optimal allocation.   (d) Competitive equilibrium with the new technology.

Step 1 · Consumer side

$U = x - \tfrac12 n$

$MRS = \dfrac{-\partial U/\partial n}{\partial U/\partial x} = \dfrac{1/2}{1} = \tfrac12$  (a number: linear utility)

Step 1 · Firm side

$x = n^{1/2}$

$MPL = \tfrac12 n^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt n}$

Step 1 · Budget (memorize)

$x = \pi + w\,n$  —  one good, price 1; income is wages plus the firm’s profit because you own the firm.

(a) Pareto optimal — branch 3A

2

Identify. “Pareto optimal” → branch A. No wage anywhere in this part.

3

$MRS = MPL$ and solve.

$$\frac12 = \frac{1}{2\sqrt n} \;\Rightarrow\; 2\sqrt n = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; \sqrt n = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; n^* = 1$$

4

Plug back. $x^* = (1)^{1/2} = 1$.

$$\boxed{n^* = 1,\quad x^* = 1}$$

(b) Competitive equilibrium — branch 3B

2

Identify. “Competitive equilibrium” → branch B. Now we need $w$ and $\pi$ too.

3

Consumer: $MRS = w$. The $MRS$ is a plain number, so this hands us the wage on the spot:

$$w = \tfrac12$$

Producer: $MPL = w$. This is the equation with $n$ in it:

$$\frac{1}{2\sqrt n} = \frac12 \;\Rightarrow\; \sqrt n = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; n^* = 1$$

4

Plug back. $x^* = 1^{1/2} = 1$, and profit last: $\pi = x^* - w n^* = 1 - \tfrac12(1) = \tfrac12$.

$$\boxed{w = \tfrac12,\quad n^* = 1,\quad x^* = 1,\quad \pi = \tfrac12}$$

Check the budget: $\pi + wn = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1 = x$ ✓. Same $(n,x)$ as part (a): the competitive equilibrium is Pareto optimal.

(c) New technology $x = n^{2/3}$ — Pareto optimal

1

Re-gather. Utility unchanged, so $MRS = \tfrac12$ still. New $MPL = \tfrac23 n^{-1/3}$.

3

$MRS = MPL$. Two fractions → multiply everything by $6$ first.

$$\frac12 = \frac23 n^{-1/3} \;\xrightarrow{\times 6}\; 3 = 4n^{-1/3} \;\Rightarrow\; n^{1/3} = \frac43 \;\Rightarrow\; n^* = \left(\frac43\right)^{3} = \frac{64}{27} \approx 2.37$$

The last move is the one to be careful with: $n^{1/3} = \tfrac43$ means you cube both sides. $\tfrac43$ is not the answer.

4

Plug back. $x^* = (n^*)^{2/3} = \left(n^{1/3}\right)^2 = \left(\tfrac43\right)^2 = \tfrac{16}{9} \approx 1.78$.

$$\boxed{n^* = \tfrac{64}{27} \approx 2.37,\quad x^* = \tfrac{16}{9} \approx 1.78}$$

(d) New technology — competitive equilibrium

3

Consumer $MRS = w$ ⇒ $w = \tfrac12$ (utility didn’t change, so neither did the wage). Producer $MPL = w$ ⇒ $\tfrac23 n^{-1/3} = \tfrac12$, which is the same equation as (c) ⇒ $n^* = \tfrac{64}{27}$.

4

Plug back. $x^* = \tfrac{16}{9}$. Profit: $\pi = x^* - wn^* = \tfrac{16}{9} - \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{64}{27} = \tfrac{48}{27} - \tfrac{32}{27} = \tfrac{16}{27} \approx 0.59$.

$$\boxed{w = \tfrac12,\quad n^* = \tfrac{64}{27},\quad x^* = \tfrac{16}{9},\quad \pi = \tfrac{16}{27}}$$

The numbers here don’t come out clean. The practice problems below use the same four steps with numbers that come out whole.

What changed with the better technology? With linear utility the wage is pinned at $MRS = \tfrac12$ no matter what the firm does. A more productive firm hires more labor at that wage ($1 \to 2.37$) and makes more output and more profit. Keep this in mind for the Cobb-Douglas practice problem, where labor behaves differently.

2

Practice — same four steps, whole-number answers

try it yourself

Every answer below is an integer. If you get a fraction, stop and look for the slip before you look at the solution.

P1.1 · linear utility, bigger numbers, exponent change

Linear utility again, new technology changes the exponent

$U(n,x) = x - 2n$. The firm produces $x = 8n^{1/2}$. $x$ is the numeraire, $w$ is the wage.

(a) Pareto optimal $n$ and $x$.   (b) Competitive equilibrium $x, n, w, \pi$.   (c) New technology $x = 6n^{2/3}$: Pareto optimal allocation.   (d) Competitive equilibrium with the new technology.

Step 1. $MRS = 2$. $MPL = 8\cdot\tfrac12 n^{-1/2} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt n}$. Budget $x = \pi + wn$.

Step 3A. $MRS = MPL$: $\;2 = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt n} \Rightarrow 2\sqrt n = 4 \Rightarrow \sqrt n = 2 \Rightarrow n^* = 4$.

Step 4. $x^* = 8\sqrt4 = 16$.

$$\boxed{n^* = 4,\quad x^* = 16}$$

Step 3B, consumer: $MRS = w \Rightarrow w = 2$ (linear utility hands you the wage).

Step 3B, producer: $MPL = w$: $\;\dfrac{4}{\sqrt n} = 2 \Rightarrow \sqrt n = 2 \Rightarrow n^* = 4$.

Step 4. $x^* = 16$. $\pi = x^* - wn^* = 16 - 2(4) = 8$. Budget check: $8 + 2(4) = 16$ ✓

$$\boxed{w = 2,\quad n^* = 4,\quad x^* = 16,\quad \pi = 8}$$

Step 1. New $MPL = 6\cdot\tfrac23 n^{-1/3} = 4n^{-1/3}$.

Step 3A. $2 = 4n^{-1/3} \Rightarrow n^{-1/3} = \tfrac12 \Rightarrow n^{1/3} = 2 \Rightarrow n^* = 2^3 = 8$.

Step 4. $x^* = 6\cdot 8^{2/3} = 6\cdot(8^{1/3})^2 = 6\cdot 4 = 24$.

$$\boxed{n^* = 8,\quad x^* = 24}$$

3B. $MRS = w \Rightarrow w = 2$. $MPL = w$: $4n^{-1/3} = 2 \Rightarrow n^* = 8$ (same equation as (c)).

4. $x^* = 24$. $\pi = 24 - 2(8) = 8$. Check: $8 + 16 = 24$ ✓

$$\boxed{w = 2,\quad n^* = 8,\quad x^* = 24,\quad \pi = 8}$$

Like the HW: wage unchanged (linear utility), labor and output up with the better technology. Profit happened to stay at 8.

P1.2 · Cobb-Douglas utility over consumption and leisure

Cobb-Douglas: the person has 12 hours; leisure is $12 - n$

$U(n,x) = x\,(12 - n)$. The firm produces $x = 4n^{1/2}$. $x$ is the numeraire, $w$ is the wage.

(a) Pareto optimal $n$ and $x$.   (b) Competitive equilibrium $x, n, w, \pi$.   (c) New technology $x = 8n^{1/2}$: Pareto optimal allocation.   (d) Competitive equilibrium with the new technology.   (e) Compare (b) and (d). What happened to labor, and why?

Step 1. $\partial U/\partial n = -x$, $\partial U/\partial x = 12 - n$, so $MRS = \dfrac{x}{12-n}$ (has variables in it this time). $MPL = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt n}$.

Step 3A. $MRS = MPL$, and plug $x = 4\sqrt n$ in so only $n$ is left:

$$\frac{4\sqrt n}{12 - n} = \frac{2}{\sqrt n} \;\Rightarrow\; 4\sqrt n\cdot\sqrt n = 2(12 - n) \;\Rightarrow\; 4n = 24 - 2n \;\Rightarrow\; 6n = 24 \;\Rightarrow\; n^* = 4$$

Step 4. $x^* = 4\sqrt 4 = 8$.

$$\boxed{n^* = 4,\quad x^* = 8}\qquad(\text{leisure } 12 - 4 = 8)$$

Step 3B. Consumer: $MRS = w$, i.e. $\dfrac{x}{12-n} = w$. Producer: $MPL = w$, i.e. $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt n} = w$. The $MRS$ is not a plain number, so write the justification:

$MRS = w$ and $MPL = w$ $\Rightarrow$ $MRS = MPL$ $\Rightarrow$ this is exactly the part (a) equation $\Rightarrow$ $n^* = 4$.

Now read the wage off either side: $w = MPL(4) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt 4} = 1$.

Step 4. $x^* = 8$. $\pi = 8 - 1(4) = 4$. Budget check: $\pi + wn = 4 + 4 = 8 = x$ ✓

$$\boxed{w = 1,\quad n^* = 4,\quad x^* = 8,\quad \pi = 4}$$

New $MPL = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt n}$. $MRS = MPL$ with $x = 8\sqrt n$:

$$\frac{8\sqrt n}{12 - n} = \frac{4}{\sqrt n} \;\Rightarrow\; 8n = 48 - 4n \;\Rightarrow\; 12n = 48 \;\Rightarrow\; n^* = 4,\qquad x^* = 8\sqrt4 = 16$$

$$\boxed{n^* = 4,\quad x^* = 16}$$

$MRS = w$ and $MPL = w$ $\Rightarrow$ $MRS = MPL$ $\Rightarrow$ $n^* = 4$ from (c). $w = MPL(4) = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$. $x^* = 16$. $\pi = 16 - 2(4) = 8$. Check: $8 + 8 = 16$ ✓

$$\boxed{w = 2,\quad n^* = 4,\quad x^* = 16,\quad \pi = 8}$$

Labor stayed at $n = 4$; wage, output and profit all doubled. That is the right answer, not a slip. With Cobb-Douglas utility over consumption and leisure, the higher wage pulls two ways: leisure got more expensive (work more), but you are richer (buy more leisure). For Cobb-Douglas these cancel exactly, so all of the productivity gain shows up as consumption. Contrast the HW’s linear utility, where labor rose.

P1.3 · quadratic disutility of labor, constant-returns firm

Quadratic cost of working, straight-line production

$U(n,x) = x - \dfrac{n^2}{4}$. The firm produces $x = 2n$. $x$ is the numeraire, $w$ is the wage.

(a) Pareto optimal $n$ and $x$.   (b) Competitive equilibrium $x, n, w, \pi$.   (c) New technology $x = 3n$: Pareto optimal allocation.   (d) Competitive equilibrium with the new technology.

Step 1. $\partial U/\partial n = -\tfrac{n}{2}$, $\partial U/\partial x = 1$, so $MRS = \dfrac{n}{2}$. $MPL = 2$ (a number: the firm is the linear one this time).

Step 3A. $\dfrac n2 = 2 \Rightarrow n^* = 4$.   Step 4. $x^* = 2(4) = 8$.

$$\boxed{n^* = 4,\quad x^* = 8}$$

Step 3B, producer: $MPL = w \Rightarrow w = 2$. This time the firm pins the wage, because its $MPL$ is a constant.

Step 3B, consumer: $MRS = w$: $\dfrac n2 = 2 \Rightarrow n^* = 4$.

Step 4. $x^* = 8$. $\pi = x^* - wn^* = 8 - 2(4) = 0$. Budget check: $0 + 2(4) = 8$ ✓

$$\boxed{w = 2,\quad n^* = 4,\quad x^* = 8,\quad \pi = 0}$$

Zero profit is correct: with constant returns, every unit of output costs exactly what it sells for, so the firm has nothing left over. All income is wages.

$MPL = 3$. $\dfrac n2 = 3 \Rightarrow n^* = 6$, $x^* = 3(6) = 18$.

$$\boxed{n^* = 6,\quad x^* = 18}$$

$MPL = w \Rightarrow w = 3$. $MRS = w \Rightarrow \dfrac n2 = 3 \Rightarrow n^* = 6$. $x^* = 18$. $\pi = 18 - 3(6) = 0$. Check: $0 + 18 = 18$ ✓

$$\boxed{w = 3,\quad n^* = 6,\quad x^* = 18,\quad \pi = 0}$$

P1.4 · Cobb-Douglas with unequal weights

Consumption counts double

$U(n,x) = x^{2}\,(18 - n)$. The firm produces $x = 6n^{1/2}$. $x$ is the numeraire, $w$ is the wage.

(a) Pareto optimal $n$ and $x$.   (b) Competitive equilibrium $x, n, w, \pi$.

Step 1. $\partial U/\partial n = -x^2$, $\partial U/\partial x = 2x(18-n)$, so $MRS = \dfrac{x^2}{2x(18-n)} = \dfrac{x}{2(18-n)}$. $MPL = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt n}$.

Step 3A. Plug $x = 6\sqrt n$:

$$\frac{6\sqrt n}{2(18-n)} = \frac{3}{\sqrt n} \;\Rightarrow\; 6n = 6(18 - n) \;\Rightarrow\; n = 18 - n \;\Rightarrow\; n^* = 9$$

Step 4. $x^* = 6\sqrt9 = 18$.

$$\boxed{n^* = 9,\quad x^* = 18}$$

$MRS = w$ and $MPL = w$ $\Rightarrow$ $MRS = MPL$ $\Rightarrow$ the part (a) equation $\Rightarrow$ $n^* = 9$. Then $w = MPL(9) = \dfrac{3}{3} = 1$, $x^* = 18$, $\pi = 18 - 1(9) = 9$. Check: $9 + 9 = 18$ ✓

$$\boxed{w = 1,\quad n^* = 9,\quad x^* = 18,\quad \pi = 9}$$

1

Worked example: System 2

worked example

Worked example 2. Labor is the only input. $x = f(L_x) = 2L_x^{1/2}$ and $y = g(L_y) = 2L_y^{1/2}$. Total labor $L = 100$.

(a) Do $f$ and $g$ exhibit decreasing, constant, or increasing returns to scale?   (b) Solve for the production possibilities frontier and draw it.

(a) Returns to scale

The exponent on the input is $\tfrac12 < 1$, so both are decreasing returns to scale. To show it: double the labor, $f(2L) = 2\sqrt{2L} = \sqrt2\cdot 2\sqrt L \approx 1.41\,f(L)$, which is less than $2f(L)$. Doubling the input less than doubles the output.

(b) The PPF

1

Start from the resource constraint. $L_x + L_y = 100$.

2

Isolate $L_x$ and $L_y$ from the production functions. Ignore the “$f(L_x)$” and just undo what was done to $L$: divide by 2, then square.

$$x = 2\sqrt{L_x} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac x2 = \sqrt{L_x} \;\Rightarrow\; L_x = \frac{x^2}{4} \qquad\qquad y = 2\sqrt{L_y} \;\Rightarrow\; L_y = \frac{y^2}{4}$$

3

Plug both into step 1.

$$\frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{y^2}{4} = 100 \;\xrightarrow{\times 4}\; x^2 + y^2 = 400$$

4

Recognize the shape. $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ with $r^2 = 400$: a circle of radius $20$. We only use the quarter with $x, y \ge 0$. (You could also write $y = \sqrt{400 - x^2}$, but the circle form is the clean answer.)

5

Intercepts by maxing out each function. All 100 workers into $x$: $x = 2\sqrt{100} = 20$. All into $y$: $y = 2\sqrt{100} = 20$. Points $(20, 0)$ and $(0, 20)$, which agree with the radius ✓

$$\boxed{x^2 + y^2 = 400,\quad 0 \le x, y \le 20}$$

Bowed out because both technologies have decreasing returns: the first workers moved into a good are the most productive ones.

Where the 400 comes from. It is not $100^2$. The constraint is on labor, $L_x + L_y = 100$; the $400$ appears only after you substitute $L_x = x^2/4$ and clear the fraction. If you can’t say where a number came from, go back to step 1 and rebuild it.

2

Practice — same five steps, different shapes

try it yourself

Each one asks the same two things: (a) returns to scale for each function, (b) the PPF with intercepts and a sketch. The shape of the curve changes with the shape of the production functions; the steps do not.

P2.1 · two square roots with different coefficients

An ellipse

$x = 2L_x^{1/2}$, $\;y = L_y^{1/2}$, $\;L = 100$.

Both exponents are $\tfrac12 < 1$: both decreasing returns to scale. The coefficient in front ($2$ or $1$) does not change returns to scale.

1. $L_x + L_y = 100$.   2. $L_x = \dfrac{x^2}{4}$, $\;L_y = y^2$.   3. $\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 100$.

4. An ellipse (a squashed circle): $y = \sqrt{100 - x^2/4}$ if you need $y$ alone.

5. Max out: $x = 2\sqrt{100} = 20$, $\;y = \sqrt{100} = 10$. Intercepts $(20,0)$ and $(0,10)$. Check a middle point: $x = 12 \Rightarrow y^2 = 100 - 36 = 64 \Rightarrow y = 8$; indeed $L_x = 36$, $L_y = 64$ add to 100 ✓

$$\boxed{\frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 100},\qquad (20,0),\ (0,10)$$

P2.2 · one linear, one square root

A parabola on its side

$x = L_x$, $\;y = 2L_y^{1/2}$, $\;L = 25$.

$x = L_x$: exponent $1$, constant returns. $y = 2L_y^{1/2}$: exponent $\tfrac12$, decreasing returns.

1. $L_x + L_y = 25$.   2. $L_x = x$ (nothing to undo), $\;L_y = \dfrac{y^2}{4}$.   3. $x + \dfrac{y^2}{4} = 25 \;\xrightarrow{\times4}\; 4x + y^2 = 100$.

4. $y^2 = 100 - 4x$, so $y = \sqrt{100 - 4x} = 2\sqrt{25 - x}$: a parabola opening to the left.

5. Max out: $x = 25$, $\;y = 2\sqrt{25} = 10$. Intercepts $(25,0)$, $(0,10)$. Middle check: $x = 16 \Rightarrow y^2 = 36 \Rightarrow y = 6$, and $16 + 9 = 25$ ✓

$$\boxed{y^2 = 100 - 4x},\qquad (25,0),\ (0,10)$$

P2.3 · both linear

A straight line

$x = 3L_x$, $\;y = 2L_y$, $\;L = 12$.

Both exponents are $1$: both constant returns to scale.

1. $L_x + L_y = 12$.   2. $L_x = \dfrac x3$, $\;L_y = \dfrac y2$.   3. $\dfrac x3 + \dfrac y2 = 12 \;\xrightarrow{\times 6}\; 2x + 3y = 72$.

4. A straight line, $y = 24 - \dfrac23 x$. Slope $-\dfrac23$: every extra unit of $x$ costs $\dfrac23$ of a unit of $y$, always.

5. Max out: $x = 3(12) = 36$, $\;y = 2(12) = 24$. Intercepts $(36,0)$, $(0,24)$. Middle: $(18, 12)$ uses $6 + 6 = 12$ workers ✓

$$\boxed{2x + 3y = 72},\qquad (36,0),\ (0,24)$$

Constant returns in both goods: the opportunity cost never changes, so no bow at all.
P2.4 · increasing returns

Bowed the other way

$x = L_x^{2}$, $\;y = L_y^{2}$, $\;L = 4$.

Exponent $2 > 1$: both increasing returns. $f(2L) = 4L^2 = 4f(L)$, so doubling labor quadruples output.

1. $L_x + L_y = 4$.   2. Undo the square: $L_x = \sqrt x$, $\;L_y = \sqrt y$.   3. $\sqrt x + \sqrt y = 4$.

4. $y = (4 - \sqrt x)^2$. This curve is bowed inward (toward the origin).

5. Max out: $x = 4^2 = 16$, $\;y = 16$. Intercepts $(16,0)$, $(0,16)$. Middle: $L_x = L_y = 2$ gives $(4,4)$, and $\sqrt4 + \sqrt4 = 4$ ✓. Compare with the straight line between the intercepts, which would pass through $(4, 12)$: splitting labor is wasteful under increasing returns.

$$\boxed{\sqrt x + \sqrt y = 4},\qquad (16,0),\ (0,16)$$

Increasing returns bow the PPF toward the origin. Specializing beats splitting.
1

Worked example: System 3

worked example

Worked example 3. $x = \min\{L_x,\, 2K_x\}$ and $y = \min\{2L_y,\, K_y\}$. Totals $L = 10$, $K = 10$; both inputs can move freely between the goods.

(a) In a production Edgeworth box, show which allocations of $L$ and $K$ are technologically efficient.   (b) Graph the PPF.

Step 0 · Firm $x$ (bottom-left origin)

$x = \min\{L_x, 2K_x\}$

Kink: $L_x = 2K_x \;\Rightarrow\; K_x = \dfrac{L_x}{2}$

Per unit of $x$: needs $L_x = x$ and $K_x = \dfrac x2$

Step 0 · Firm $y$ (top-right origin)

$y = \min\{2L_y, K_y\}$

Kink: $2L_y = K_y$

Per unit of $y$: needs $L_y = \dfrac y2$ and $K_y = y$

Step 0 · Totals and the one cross-over

$L = 10$, $K = 10$. Box is $10$ wide by $10$ tall. $\;L_y = 10 - L_x$, $\;K_y = 10 - K_x$. That is the only place firm $y$’s letters touch firm $x$’s.

(a) Technologically efficient allocations

1

Kink lines in each firm’s own letters. A $\min$ firm wastes nothing only when the two things inside are equal.

$$\text{firm } x:\; K_x = \tfrac12 L_x \qquad\qquad \text{firm } y:\; K_y = 2L_y$$

2

Put firm $y$’s line into firm $x$’s letters using the cross-over once.

$$10 - K_x = 2(10 - L_x) \;\Rightarrow\; 10 - K_x = 20 - 2L_x \;\Rightarrow\; K_x = 2L_x - 10$$

Sanity check the line: at $L_x = 10$ it gives $K_x = 10$, the top-right corner, which is firm $y$’s origin ✓.

3

Intersect the two lines. Fractions on one side → multiply by 2.

$$\tfrac12 L_x = 2L_x - 10 \;\xrightarrow{\times 2}\; L_x = 4L_x - 20 \;\Rightarrow\; 3L_x = 20 \;\Rightarrow\; L_x = \tfrac{20}{3},\quad K_x = \tfrac{10}{3}$$

Firm $y$ gets the rest: $L_y = \tfrac{10}{3}$, $K_y = \tfrac{20}{3}$. Check nobody wastes: $x = \min\{\tfrac{20}{3}, \tfrac{20}{3}\}$ and $y = \min\{\tfrac{20}{3}, \tfrac{20}{3}\}$ ✓

The one allocation where neither firm wastes anything: $$(L_x, K_x) = \left(\tfrac{20}{3}, \tfrac{10}{3}\right),\qquad (L_y, K_y) = \left(\tfrac{10}{3}, \tfrac{20}{3}\right)$$

What to shade. Efficient means “you can’t raise one output without lowering the other.” Between the two kink lines both firms are short of the same input, so the spare units of the other input are useless to everybody and there is no trade that helps. That gives two wedges (the bow-tie in the figure) meeting at the no-waste point. Outside the wedges one firm has spare $L$ while the other has spare $K$; swap them and both outputs rise, so those allocations are not efficient.

(b) The PPF

4

One line per input. Use the per-unit needs from step 0.

$$L:\; L_x + L_y = 10 \;\Rightarrow\; x + \frac y2 = 10 \;\Rightarrow\; y = 20 - 2x$$ $$K:\; K_x + K_y = 10 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac x2 + y = 10 \;\Rightarrow\; y = 10 - \frac x2$$

5

Intercepts by maxing out. Everything into $x$: $x = \min\{10, 20\} = 10$. Everything into $y$: $y = \min\{20, 10\} = 10$. The kink is where the two lines cross:

$$20 - 2x = 10 - \tfrac x2 \;\xrightarrow{\times 2}\; 40 - 4x = 20 - x \;\Rightarrow\; 3x = 20 \;\Rightarrow\; x = \tfrac{20}{3},\; y = \tfrac{20}{3}$$

Same numbers as the no-waste point’s outputs, as they must be.

6

PPF = the lower of the two lines.

$$\boxed{\;y = \begin{cases} 10 - \tfrac12 x, & 0 \le x \le \tfrac{20}{3} \quad(K \text{ is the bottleneck})\\[4pt] 20 - 2x, & \tfrac{20}{3} \le x \le 10 \quad(L \text{ is the bottleneck})\end{cases}}$$

From $(0,10)$ down a gentle slope of $-\tfrac12$ to the kink at $\left(\tfrac{20}{3},\tfrac{20}{3}\right)$, then steeply at $-2$ to $(10,0)$.

Why two lines? Each input gives its own “budget line” for outputs. Only one of them binds at a time — the scarce one — so the economy lives on whichever line is lower. The kink is where the scarce input switches from $K$ to $L$.

2

Practice — same six steps, whole-number kinks

try it yourself
P3.1 · same box, firm $y$ is more labor-hungry

Change one coefficient

$x = \min\{L_x, 2K_x\}$, $\;y = \min\{3L_y, K_y\}$, $\;L = 10$, $K = 10$. (a) Efficient allocations in the box. (b) The PPF.

0. Per unit: $x$ needs $L_x = x$, $K_x = \dfrac x2$. $\;y$ needs $L_y = \dfrac y3$, $K_y = y$. Cross-over $L_y = 10 - L_x$, $K_y = 10 - K_x$.

1. Kinks: $K_x = \dfrac{L_x}{2}$; $\;K_y = 3L_y$.

2. Firm $y$ in $x$’s letters: $10 - K_x = 3(10 - L_x) \Rightarrow K_x = 3L_x - 20$.

3. Intersect: $\dfrac{L_x}{2} = 3L_x - 20 \xrightarrow{\times2} L_x = 6L_x - 40 \Rightarrow 5L_x = 40 \Rightarrow L_x = 8,\; K_x = 4$. Firm $y$: $L_y = 2$, $K_y = 6$. Check: $x = \min\{8,8\}$, $y = \min\{6,6\}$ ✓

$$\boxed{(L_x,K_x) = (8,4),\quad (L_y,K_y) = (2,6)}$$ plus the two wedges between the kink lines.

4. $L$ line: $x + \dfrac y3 = 10 \Rightarrow y = 30 - 3x$. $\;K$ line: $\dfrac x2 + y = 10 \Rightarrow y = 10 - \dfrac x2$.

5. Max out: $x_{\max} = \min\{10, 20\} = 10$; $y_{\max} = \min\{30, 10\} = 10$. Kink: $30 - 3x = 10 - \dfrac x2 \xrightarrow{\times2} 60 - 6x = 20 - x \Rightarrow 5x = 40 \Rightarrow x = 8,\; y = 6$.

6. Lower line wins.

$$\boxed{y = \begin{cases}10 - \tfrac12 x, & 0\le x\le 8\\ 30 - 3x, & 8 \le x \le 10\end{cases}}\qquad (0,10),\ (8,6),\ (10,0)$$

P3.2 · mirror image, bigger box

Firm $x$ is the capital-hungry one

$x = \min\{2L_x, K_x\}$, $\;y = \min\{L_y, 2K_y\}$, $\;L = 12$, $K = 12$. (a) Efficient allocations. (b) The PPF.

0. Per unit: $x$ needs $L_x = \dfrac x2$, $K_x = x$. $\;y$ needs $L_y = y$, $K_y = \dfrac y2$. Cross-over $L_y = 12 - L_x$, $K_y = 12 - K_x$.

1. Kinks: $K_x = 2L_x$; $\;L_y = 2K_y$.

2. Firm $y$ in $x$’s letters: $12 - L_x = 2(12 - K_x) \Rightarrow 12 - L_x = 24 - 2K_x \Rightarrow K_x = \dfrac{L_x}{2} + 6$.

3. Intersect: $2L_x = \dfrac{L_x}{2} + 6 \xrightarrow{\times 2} 4L_x = L_x + 12 \Rightarrow L_x = 4,\; K_x = 8$. Firm $y$: $L_y = 8$, $K_y = 4$. Check: $x = \min\{8,8\}$, $y = \min\{8,8\}$ ✓

$$\boxed{(L_x,K_x) = (4,8),\quad (L_y,K_y) = (8,4)}$$ plus the two wedges between the kink lines.

4. $L$ line: $\dfrac x2 + y = 12 \Rightarrow y = 12 - \dfrac x2$. $\;K$ line: $x + \dfrac y2 = 12 \Rightarrow y = 24 - 2x$.

5. Max out: $x_{\max} = \min\{24, 12\} = 12$; $y_{\max} = \min\{12, 24\} = 12$. Kink: $12 - \dfrac x2 = 24 - 2x \xrightarrow{\times2} 24 - x = 48 - 4x \Rightarrow 3x = 24 \Rightarrow x = 8,\; y = 8$.

$$\boxed{y = \begin{cases}12 - \tfrac12 x, & 0\le x\le 8\\ 24 - 2x, & 8 \le x \le 12\end{cases}}\qquad (0,12),\ (8,8),\ (12,0)$$

P3.3 · box is not square

Unequal totals

$x = \min\{L_x, K_x\}$, $\;y = \min\{L_y, 3K_y\}$, $\;L = 12$, $K = 8$. (a) Efficient allocations. (b) The PPF.

0. Per unit: $x$ needs $L_x = x$, $K_x = x$. $\;y$ needs $L_y = y$, $K_y = \dfrac y3$. Box is $12$ wide, $8$ tall. Cross-over $L_y = 12 - L_x$, $K_y = 8 - K_x$.

1. Kinks: $K_x = L_x$; $\;L_y = 3K_y$.

2. Firm $y$ in $x$’s letters: $12 - L_x = 3(8 - K_x) = 24 - 3K_x \Rightarrow K_x = \dfrac{L_x + 12}{3}$.

3. Intersect: $L_x = \dfrac{L_x + 12}{3} \xrightarrow{\times3} 3L_x = L_x + 12 \Rightarrow L_x = 6,\; K_x = 6$. Firm $y$: $L_y = 6$, $K_y = 2$. Check: $x = \min\{6,6\}$, $y = \min\{6, 6\}$ ✓

$$\boxed{(L_x,K_x) = (6,6),\quad (L_y,K_y) = (6,2)}$$ plus the two wedges between the kink lines.

4. $L$ line: $x + y = 12$. $\;K$ line: $x + \dfrac y3 = 8 \Rightarrow y = 24 - 3x$.

5. Max out: $x_{\max} = \min\{12, 8\} = 8$; $y_{\max} = \min\{12, 24\} = 12$. Kink: $12 - x = 24 - 3x \Rightarrow 2x = 12 \Rightarrow x = 6,\; y = 6$.

$$\boxed{y = \begin{cases}12 - x, & 0\le x\le 6\\ 24 - 3x, & 6 \le x \le 8\end{cases}}\qquad (0,12),\ (6,6),\ (8,0)$$

1

Worked example: System 4

worked example

Worked example 4. $x = \min\{L_x,\, 2K_x\}$ and $y = 2L_y + K_y$. Totals $L = 12$, $K = 6$; both inputs can move freely between the goods.

(a) In a production Edgeworth box, show which allocations are technologically efficient.   (b) Graph the PPF.

Step 0 · Firm $x$ (Leontief, bottom-left origin)

$x = \min\{L_x, 2K_x\}$   Kink: $K_x = \dfrac{L_x}{2}$

Per unit of $x$: $L_x = x$, $\;K_x = \dfrac x2$

Step 0 · Firm $y$ (linear, top-right origin)

$y = 2L_y + K_y$   No kink. Each unit of $L$ is worth $2$ units of $y$, each unit of $K$ is worth $1$.

Uses whatever is left over, nothing wasted.

Step 0 · Totals and the one cross-over

$L = 12$, $K = 6$. Box is $12$ wide by $6$ tall. $\;L_y = 12 - L_x$, $\;K_y = 6 - K_x$.

(a) Technologically efficient allocations

1

Kink line for the Leontief firm: $K_x = \tfrac12 L_x$. Off this line firm $x$ is wasting some $L$ or some $K$ — and firm $y$ can always use either one. So anything off the line can be improved, and the efficient allocations are exactly the kink line.

2

Does it reach the far corner? At $L_x = 12$ the line needs $K_x = 6$, which is exactly all the capital. So it runs from firm $x$’s origin straight to firm $y$’s origin: the diagonal of the box.

$$\boxed{\text{Efficient allocations: } K_x = \tfrac12 L_x,\quad 0 \le L_x \le 12}$$

(b) The PPF

3

Write firm $x$’s inputs in terms of $x$, hand the rest to firm $y$.

$$L_x = x,\; K_x = \frac x2 \;\Rightarrow\; L_y = 12 - x,\; K_y = 6 - \frac x2$$ $$y = 2L_y + K_y = 2(12 - x) + \left(6 - \frac x2\right) = 30 - \frac52 x$$

4

Check both ends by maxing out. All inputs to $y$: $y = 2(12) + 6 = 30$ ✓ matches the intercept. All inputs to $x$: $x = \min\{12, 2\cdot 6\} = 12$, and the line gives $y = 30 - \tfrac52(12) = 0$ ✓

$$\boxed{y = 30 - \tfrac52 x,\quad 0 \le x \le 12}\qquad (0,30),\ (12,0)$$

A straight line with slope $-\tfrac52$: one more unit of $x$ eats $1$ unit of $L$ (worth $2$ units of $y$) and $\tfrac12$ unit of $K$ (worth $\tfrac12$ unit of $y$). $2 + \tfrac12 = \tfrac52$.

2

Practice — same four steps

try it yourself
P4.1 · capital-hungry Leontief, equal-weight linear

Taller box

$x = \min\{2L_x, K_x\}$, $\;y = L_y + K_y$, $\;L = 6$, $K = 12$. (a) Efficient allocations. (b) The PPF.

1. Kink: $K_x = 2L_x$.   2. At $L_x = 6$ it needs $K_x = 12 = K$: corner to corner. Firm $y$ is linear, so it absorbs any leftovers.

$$\boxed{K_x = 2L_x,\quad 0\le L_x \le 6}$$

3. Per unit of $x$: $L_x = \dfrac x2$, $K_x = x$. Leftovers $L_y = 6 - \dfrac x2$, $K_y = 12 - x$. $\;y = \left(6 - \dfrac x2\right) + (12 - x) = 18 - \dfrac32 x$.

4. Max out: $y_{\max} = 6 + 12 = 18$ ✓; $x_{\max} = \min\{12, 12\} = 12$, and $18 - \dfrac32(12) = 0$ ✓

$$\boxed{y = 18 - \tfrac32 x,\quad 0\le x\le 12}\qquad (0,18),\ (12,0)$$

P4.2 · one-to-one Leontief, capital counts double for $y$

Integer slope

$x = \min\{L_x, K_x\}$, $\;y = L_y + 2K_y$, $\;L = 10$, $K = 10$. (a) Efficient allocations. (b) The PPF.

1. Kink: $K_x = L_x$.   2. At $L_x = 10$ it needs $K_x = 10 = K$: the diagonal, corner to corner.

$$\boxed{K_x = L_x,\quad 0\le L_x\le 10}$$

3. $L_x = x$, $K_x = x$ $\Rightarrow$ $L_y = 10 - x$, $K_y = 10 - x$ $\Rightarrow$ $y = (10 - x) + 2(10 - x) = 30 - 3x$.

4. Max out: $y_{\max} = 10 + 20 = 30$ ✓; $x_{\max} = \min\{10,10\} = 10$ and $30 - 30 = 0$ ✓

$$\boxed{y = 30 - 3x,\quad 0\le x\le 10}\qquad (0,30),\ (10,0)$$

P4.3 · roles swapped: $x$ is linear, $y$ is Leontief

The Leontief firm is on top now

$x = L_x + K_x$, $\;y = \min\{L_y, 2K_y\}$, $\;L = 12$, $K = 6$. (a) Efficient allocations. (b) The PPF.

1. The kink belongs to firm $y$ this time, in firm $y$’s own letters: $L_y = 2K_y$.   2. At $K_y = 6$ it needs $L_y = 12 = L$: it reaches the far corner (firm $x$’s origin). The efficient allocations are firm $y$’s kink line; firm $x$ (linear) takes the leftovers.

If you want it in $x$’s letters: $12 - L_x = 2(6 - K_x) \Rightarrow L_x = 2K_x$, the same diagonal.

$$\boxed{L_y = 2K_y,\quad 0 \le K_y \le 6}$$

3. Per unit of $y$: $L_y = y$, $K_y = \dfrac y2$. Leftovers to $x$: $x = (12 - y) + \left(6 - \dfrac y2\right) = 18 - \dfrac32 y$. Solve for $y$ if you like: $y = 12 - \dfrac23 x$.

4. Max out: $x_{\max} = 12 + 6 = 18$ ✓; $y_{\max} = \min\{12, 12\} = 12$ ✓

$$\boxed{x = 18 - \tfrac32 y \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; y = 12 - \tfrac23 x}\qquad (18,0),\ (0,12)$$

3

Two stretch problems

optional
P4.4 (stretch) · the kink line does not reach the corner

Capital runs out first

$x = \min\{L_x, K_x\}$, $\;y = L_y + K_y$, $\;L = 10$, $K = 6$. (a) Efficient allocations. (b) The PPF.

1. Kink: $K_x = L_x$.   2. At $L_x = 10$ it would need $K_x = 10$, but there are only $6$. The line hits the top of the box at $(6,6)$ and stops. Past that, firm $x$ cannot grow: $x_{\max} = \min\{10, 6\} = 6$.

$$\boxed{K_x = L_x,\quad 0 \le L_x \le 6}$$ (the diagonal from firm $x$’s origin to the top edge, not to the corner)

3. $L_x = K_x = x$ $\Rightarrow$ $y = (10 - x) + (6 - x) = 16 - 2x$, but only for $0 \le x \le 6$.

4. Max out: $y_{\max} = 16$ ✓. At $x = 6$: $y = 16 - 12 = 4$, not zero — the $4$ units of labor firm $x$ can’t use still go to firm $y$. The frontier ends at $(6, 4)$; the feasible set then drops straight down to $(6, 0)$, but points on that vertical edge waste labor and are not efficient.

$$\boxed{y = 16 - 2x,\quad 0\le x\le 6}\qquad (0,16) \text{ to } (6,4)$$

P4.5 (stretch) · both firms linear

No kink lines at all: compare opportunity costs

$x = 2L_x + K_x$, $\;y = L_y + 2K_y$, $\;L = 10$, $K = 10$. (a) Efficient allocations. (b) The PPF.

Neither firm has a kink, so there is no line to find. Instead compare what each input is worth to each firm. A unit of $L$ makes $2$ units of $x$ or $1$ unit of $y$: it is relatively better at $x$. A unit of $K$ makes $1$ unit of $x$ or $2$ units of $y$: relatively better at $y$.

Efficiency says: give each firm the input it is relatively good with first. Starting from “all to $y$,” move labor to $x$ until labor is gone (bottom edge of the box, $K_x = 0$), then move capital (right edge, $L_x = 10$).

$$\boxed{\text{bottom edge } K_x = 0,\ 0\le L_x\le 10,\ \text{ then right edge } L_x = 10,\ 0\le K_x\le 10}$$

Corner of the path ($L_x = 10, K_x = 0$): $x = 20$, $y = 0 + 2(10) = 20$. Ends: all to $y$ gives $(0, 30)$; all to $x$ gives $(30, 0)$.

First segment (moving labor): each unit of $L$ gives $+2x$ and $-1y$, slope $-\tfrac12$: $y = 30 - \tfrac12 x$ for $0 \le x \le 20$. Second segment (moving capital): $+1x$, $-2y$, slope $-2$: $y = 60 - 2x$ for $20 \le x \le 30$.

$$\boxed{y = \begin{cases}30 - \tfrac12 x, & 0 \le x \le 20\\ 60 - 2x, & 20 \le x \le 30\end{cases}}\qquad (0,30),\ (20,20),\ (30,0)$$

Still bowed outward, like the Leontief + Leontief PPF, but for a different reason: there the slope changed because the scarce input switched; here it changes because the input being moved switches from the cheap one to the expensive one.
